cues.text: Section five: Compliance and data protection.
Let us begin with what compliance actually means.
Compliance means meeting applicable laws, regulations, contractual requirements and internal policies.
Notice that this covers more than the law alone: it includes the promises an organisation makes in contracts and the rules it sets for itself.
Three things work together here.
Governance sets responsibility for compliance, so that someone is clearly accountable.
Controls enforce the requirements in day-to-day operations.
And audits collect evidence that the requirements are actually being met.
Ethics goes beyond minimum legal obligations.

A technically lawful practice can still be unfair or harmful, so a responsible professional asks not only "Is this allowed?" but also "Is this right?" Now let us look at specific frameworks, starting with the GDPR.
The GDPR protects personal data within its applicable territorial scope, which means it does not apply everywhere by default.
Its principles include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security and accountability.
Consent is one lawful basis for processing, but it is not the only one.
Individuals also have rights, such as access, rectification and erasure, subject to applicable conditions.
Next, HIPAA.
This is a United States law governing protected health information in covered entities and relevant business associates.
Its Privacy Rule, Security Rule and Breach Notification Rule address, respectively, permitted use, safeguards and notification.
Importantly, HIPAA does not automatically apply to every hospital worldwide.
Turning to Nigeria.
The course book discusses the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation, or NDPR.
For contemporary Nigerian practice, you should also recognise the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, known as the NDPC.
Do not assume the older regulation alone describes the current legal regime.
In general terms, organisations need a lawful basis, appropriate safeguards, transparency, processes for data subject rights, and accountability.
Please remember that this is conceptual teaching, not a current legal compliance opinion.
Another name you will meet is PCI DSS.
This is an industry security standard for payment card data.
It is not a general privacy law.
More broadly, regulatory requirements depend on jurisdiction, sector and the data processed.
Let us now consider practical controls.
These include data classification, least privilege, encryption in transit and at rest, retention schedules, audit logging, vendor due diligence, staff training and incident response.
One example worth understanding is the consent management system.
It records what a person agreed to, when they agreed, for what purpose, and whether consent was later withdrawn.
It is useful only where consent is the relevant lawful basis.
Finally, two roles you must distinguish.
A data controller determines the purposes and means of processing.
A processor handles data on behalf of a controller.
Outsourcing does not remove accountability: the controller remains responsible even when a processor does the work.
For that reason, contracts should specify security obligations, incident reporting, data handling and exit arrangements.
